title: NASA Administrator: We Are Not a Procurement Agency, We Are a Nuclear-Powered NASA
dek: Jared Isaacman says NASA used to spread resources across every congressional district and partner for partnership's sake, and the result is a lunar rocket less efficient than the Saturn V; what he wants to build is nuclear power and nuclear propulsion, and to hand low Earth orbit to companies like SpaceX.
why: This is the policy manifesto of NASA's new administrator, with information density concentrated on the lunar south pole, nuclear power and the Mars plan, though the back half of the interview is soft and the Q&A quality is middling.
who: Founders and investors watching space, deep tech investment and geopolitical competition; anyone who wants to know where NASA's new administrator will put money and which capabilities will be outsourced to companies like SpaceX.
skip: The Q&A from 32:43 to 35:28 is soft and can be fast-forwarded.

points.h: NASA used to spread resources thin to please everyone
points.body: Isaacman sorts NASA's problems into two categories: externally imposed and self-inflicted. Partnering for partnership's sake turned partnerships into a drag on missions rather than an accelerator. The result is that Orion cannot inject into low lunar orbit the way Apollo did; the previous administration cancelled Mars Sample Return because the cost would exceed an aircraft carrier. He also says NASA built programs that are "too big to fail and too expensive to ever really succeed," counting on them to survive across administrations. Core capabilities were rented out, outsourced or simply lost, and progress that should have taken months turned into years at greatly increased cost.

points.h: The lunar rocket is less efficient than the Saturn V of sixty years ago
points.body: He offers a jarring comparison: China's rockets were designed when locomotives still burned coal, and today China operates 25,000 miles of high-speed rail and is only a few years from its own Apollo 11 moment. Yet NASA's lunar rocket is less efficient than the Saturn V at converting launch mass into payload headed to the Moon; the gap between Artemis 1 and Artemis 2 is longer than all 12 Gemini missions of sixty years ago combined. The lunar space station puts astronauts in a position to look down on the most coveted lunar real estate rather than working on the surface and occupying it.

points.h: The lunar south pole has only a few good parking spots
points.body: The Moon's surface area is roughly that of Africa, but the south pole is only about the size of Washington, D.C., and the usable permanently shadowed craters are limited. Those craters hold water ice, and the environment is harsher than Mars itself; the crater walls can also provide near-permanent solar illumination. So good landing sites are very few. He notes that a Starship-sized vehicle landing on the lunar surface will blast out a crater and throw debris, further shrinking the usable spots. China's robotic mission is targeting Shackleton Crater next year, and China and Russia are also cooperating on a nuclear-powered lunar base.

NASA is saying goodbye to failed nuclear programs that have not left the lab since 1965, and in 2028 will launch SR1 Freedom, a 100-kilowatt fission reactor. The mission will fly past Mars and release Skyfall, carrying three Ingenuity-class helicopters to scout subsurface ice and future landing sites with ground-penetrating radar. He calls this the beginning of a "nuclear-powered NASA," turning its workforce and facilities back to missions that are nearly impossible and have no obvious commercial case. SR2, SR3 and SR4 will follow, with targets including Enceladus, Europa and Titan, moons with oceans and complex chemistry.

points.h: The hardest part of Mars is not getting there, it is coming back
points.body: Pure chemical propulsion can also send astronauts to Mars, at a speed comparable to going to the Moon, and the habitation problem was solved long ago. The hard part is how to come back: you need to manufacture propellant on the Martian surface, and the plan is robots plus football-field-sized solar arrays, with the dust accumulated by dust storms periodically blown off. He says doing this under one atmosphere and 1G on Earth is already extremely difficult. NASA's answer is to stop doing what industry already does well and turn to next-generation capabilities with no commercial case: fission power, plus a chemically enhanced nuclear transfer vehicle using krypton or xenon rather than manufacturing propellant on the Martian surface.

points.h: Hiring is not hard, retaining talent is
points.body: NASA's internship program accepts only 1% of applicants, so there is no recruiting problem at first. The question is whether it can keep people. If NASA does the same things as SpaceX, Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, Stoke and ULA while still flying fifty-year-old space shuttle hardware, it will lose talent. His approach: once a breakthrough has a commercial case, such as launch, NASA becomes one customer among many, hands the capability to industry and moves on to the next new thing. SR1 is only the beginning of a nuclear-powered NASA, their Nautilus, and a whole nuclear-powered fleet will follow.

points.h: Nuclear propulsion is essentially an ion thruster in space
points.body: He explains the principle: the ion thrusters on Starlink satellites generate power from solar arrays, ionize and accelerate krypton or xenon and expel it, giving extremely high exhaust velocity, very low thrust but very high efficiency, so propellant lasts a long time. The farther you get from the Sun, the more useless solar power becomes, and near Jupiter it is essentially negligible. At that point you switch to the heat of a nuclear reactor, starting at 100 kilowatts and possibly scaling to 250 kilowatts or even megawatts. The reactor should run as hot as possible, using high-temperature materials and a closed Brayton cycle to convert heat into electricity, then drive the same thrusters, just scaled up from 12, 14, 25 kilowatts.

points.h: NASA does not lack budget, it lacks capital allocation ability
points.body: He says NASA does not have a top line problem, but has long been bad at capital allocation, partly by NASA's own choice and partly imposed by others. The budget is now $25 billion. He asks how many founders are in the room, saying $25 billion is a lot of money and can build rather astonishing hardware. In aeronautics, he complains that NASA's aeronautics budget is used to subsidize high-TRL programs at big contractors, such as a forty-year-old engine that wants another 3% fuel efficiency and gets NASA to pay for it. He wants to return to radical airframe and engine designs.
